principles: Never weaken review integrity: the gate and bindings stay byte-for-byte unchanged; the framework never skips a reviewer.
Surface information, let the human decide: expose scope-change + the already-existing round-2+ leniency, do not automate skipping.
Reuse existing round/diff/headHash machinery; do not duplicate or fork gate logic.
Stay read-only and additive: a helper, a CLI, and an advisory line -- nothing that can alter a transition result.
drivers: Re-review rounds re-analyze the whole diff from scratch even when little changed since a reviewer last passed.
The round-2+ gate is already lenient (>=1 receipt), but operators do not know it and there is no signal of which reviewers' scope changed.
All inputs (bound headHash, changed-files-between) already exist, so this is cheap and additive.

options.name: Option 2 merged: incremental context helper + round-2+ informed targeted re-review guidance
pros: Zero added under-review risk: gate unchanged, no reviewer ever skipped by the framework.
Cuts real cost: cheaper per-reviewer re-runs AND unlocks the already-legal round-2+ targeted path with information support.
cons: Targeted re-review stays an operator judgement (same under-review responsibility as today).
Saving is per-reviewer work + informed operator choice, not framework automation.

options.name: Skip variant: framework carries forward unaffected reviewers
pros: Largest automation: the framework itself skips reviewers whose scope did not change.
cons: Irreducible under-review risk: an LLM reviewer's true dependency set is not statically provable, so a wrong scope guess silently ships a regression.
Requires changing the gate / binding semantics and an audited carry-forward path.

options.name: Do nothing: rely on converge-fixes discipline + the B-cfdd advisory
cons: Each re-run still redoes full analysis; the round-2+ leniency stays hidden, so operators keep over-running reviewers.

chosen: Option 2 merged: incremental context helper + round-2+ informed targeted re-review guidance
rationale: Option 2 cuts the real re-review cost with a read-only, gate-unchanged, additive change and zero added under-review risk, while unlocking an already-legal round-2+ path with information support. The skip variant is rejected because its under-review risk cannot be reduced to zero (LLM dependency sets are not statically provable). Do-nothing leaves redundant full re-analysis and a hidden leniency.

preMortem.scenario: The advisory or helper is mistaken for a framework instruction to skip reviewers, leading to under-review.
preMortem.trigger: The wording implies the framework decides which reviewers to skip.
preMortem.consequence: An operator skips a reviewer that should have re-run; a regression ships.
preMortem.mitigation: Word the advisory explicitly as an operator judgement ('you MAY', 'the framework skips nobody, this is your call'); the gate is unchanged so a genuinely-needed reviewer's absence still surfaces via the normal round-1/blocking-finding paths; CHK-003 asserts the gate is untouched.

preMortem.scenario: The helper accidentally mutates state or affects a transition (not truly read-only).
preMortem.trigger: The CLI or transition-effects injection writes or throws.
preMortem.consequence: A read-only feature changes gate/transition behavior.
preMortem.mitigation: Implement the helper as a pure read over the store; inject the advisory in a try/catch append-only block (like B-cfdd); CHK-003 asserts canPassReviewGuard behaves identically with and without the helper.

preMortem.scenario: scopeChanged is computed wrongly (renames/moves missed, or wrong baseline commit), misleading the operator.
preMortem.trigger: Using plain --name-only without -M, or diffing from the wrong headHash.
preMortem.consequence: The operator re-runs the wrong set, or wrongly believes nothing changed.
preMortem.mitigation: Diff from the reviewer's recorded last-pass headHash using --name-status -M (rename-aware), reusing evidence-freshness.changedFilesBetween; fall back to full diff when no prior pass; cover a rename case in the smoke.
